report.headline: AIM-HIGH (3,414 patients) was stopped early for futility after the DSMB found less than a 1 in 10,000 chance of ever showing significant benefit; the trial's explicit hypothesis — incremental benefit from raising HDL-C on top of statin therapy — was doomed because HDL-C is not causal for coronary artery disease.
report.summary: The AIM-HIGH trial randomized 3,414 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and optimally treated LDL-C (baseline 71 mg/dL on simvastatin) to extended-release niacin or placebo, with baseline HDL-C of 34.9 mg/dL and triglycerides of 161 mg/dL. The primary endpoint was a composite of coronary heart disease death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, hospitalization for acute coronary syndrome, or symptom-driven coronary or cerebral revascularization. The trial was designed for 850 events with 85% power to detect a 25% relative risk reduction based on HDL-C raising, but it was stopped early on 2011-05-26 because the DSMB judged the chance of eventual benefit to be less than 1 in 10,000. The calculator estimates an expected hazard ratio of 0.928 (7.2% RRR) based on LDL-C lowering of 0.338 mmol/L (from -18.4% on baseline 1.836 mmol/L), yielding only 19.2% power against a minimum detectable HR of 0.825 for 80% power. The primary explanation is biomarker_not_causal: the intended biomarker (HDL-C) is non-causal for coronary artery disease, and the trial's explicit rationale was to test incremental benefit from raising HDL-C. The LDL-C lowering effect is real but too small to power the trial, making effect_too_small a valid secondary factor.
key_evidence: 3,414 patients randomized (The role of niacin in raising high-density lipoprotein cholesterol to reduce cardiovascular events... Rationale and study design... (AIM-HIGH); NHLBI: Questions and Answers: AIM-HIGH Study (dated May 26, 2011); ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00120289)

Median follow-up 4.1 years at stop (The role of niacin in raising high-density lipoprotein cholesterol... baseline characteristics... (AIM-HIGH) trial); 32 months actual follow-up at stop (NHLBI: Questions and Answers: AIM-HIGH Study (dated May 26, 2011))

report.what_would_change_this: Full publication of AIM-HIGH results with an observed hazard ratio, confidence interval, and placebo-adjusted on-treatment changes in HDL-C, LDL-C, triglycerides, and Lp(a) could revise the effect-size estimate, though the DSMB's futility boundary makes a meaningful benefit highly unlikely.
report.readthrough_note: The same biomarker-not-causal logic applies to other HDL-raising programmes; HPS2-THRIVE (niacin/laropiprant) also failed and showed excess non-fatal serious adverse events, reinforcing that HDL-C elevation is not a valid causal target for cardiovascular risk reduction.

mechanism.notes: AIM-HIGH stopped early for futility on 2011-05-26 (cut-off date). Biomarker changes from placebo-adjusted phase 2 trial (ERN/LRPT, pmid:19166443) at 2g dose, as AIM-HIGH's own biomarker data (announcement, pmcid:PMC3120226) are within-arm only. Phase 2 background therapy not specified; AIM-HIGH used niacin added to simvastatin. Median follow-up: 4.1 years per NEJM (pmcid:PMC3120223), though announcement cites 32 months. Planned events: 850. No genetic evidence for GPR109A/HM74A target. Intended biomarker: HDL-C (non-causal per reference table).

for.text: The trial's explicit rationale was to test incremental benefit of raising HDL-C on top of statin therapy (readout statement: 'determine whether there is incremental clinical benefit of niacin in reducing cardiovascular events in patients who have attained optimal on-treatment levels of LDL-C with a statin').
Calculator input confirms intended_biomarker is HDL-C.
Reference table (per system knowledge) states HDL-C causal=no for coronary artery disease.
Niacin raised HDL-C by 20% (placebo-adjusted phase 2 at 2g dose) and 15-30% (within-arm phase 3), confirming biomarker engagement.

against.text: Niacin also lowers causal biomarkers: LDL-C (-18.4% placebo-adjusted phase 2), triglycerides (-25.8%), Lp(a) (-20.8%), apoB (-18.8%), non-HDL-C (-19.8%).

hypotheses.would_settle: Genetic evidence already establishes HDL-C as non-causal; no further data needed.

for.text: Calculator estimates expected HR 0.928 (7.2% RRR) based on LDL-C lowering of 0.338 mmol/L (from -18.4% on baseline 1.836 mmol/L = 71 mg/dL).
Trial was powered for 25% RRR (assumed_rrr 25%), but expected effect is only 7.2% RRR.
Minimum detectable effect for 80% power is HR 0.825; expected HR 0.928 yields only 19.2% power.
Planned events 850, median follow-up 4.1 years (32 months at stop).

against.text: If HDL-C were causal, expected benefit would be larger; the small effect reflects LDL-C already at 71 mg/dL on statin, leaving little room for further LDL lowering.

hypotheses.would_settle: A trial powered for 7% RRR would require ~30,000 patients and longer follow-up.

for.text: Target genetics listed as 'uncertain' — no genetic evidence found for niacin's target (GPR109A/HM74A) and coronary artery disorder.

against.text: 'Uncertain' differs from 'not_causal'; absence of genetic evidence for a well-studied target does not prove the target is invalid, only that evidence is lacking.

hypotheses.would_settle: Mendelian randomization studies of GPR109A variants and CHD outcomes.

for.text: Niacin associated with cystoid maculopathy at high doses (3-4.5 g daily).
ERN/LRPT phase 2 study noted a safety signal (boolean=1).

against.text: AIM-HIGH used 1-2 g daily, below doses linked to maculopathy.
Trial stopped for futility, not safety; no evidence harm offset benefit.

hypotheses.would_settle: Full safety data from AIM-HIGH (not yet published as of 2011-05-26).

for.text: Patients had very low baseline LDL-C (71 mg/dL) on simvastatin, so additional LDL lowering has diminishing absolute benefit.
Inclusion required LDL-C 40-80 mg/dL and HDL-C ≤40/50 mg/dL, TG 150-400 mg/dL — a residual-risk population.

against.text: Calculator already incorporates baseline LDL-C and on-treatment change; population effect is captured in the effect size estimate.

hypotheses.would_settle: Subgroup analysis by baseline LDL-C tertiles (not available as of 2011-05-26).

for.text: Primary endpoint includes symptom-driven revascularization, a soft endpoint less sensitive to lipid modification.
Trial stopped early at median 32 months follow-up vs planned longer duration.

against.text: Calculator uses 4.1 years follow-up and 850 events (planned), not the truncated data.
Composite endpoint standard for cardiovascular outcomes trials.

hypotheses.would_settle: Component-specific analysis of hard vs soft endpoints (not available).

against.text: Stopped for futility (scientific reason), not business decision or poor execution.

for.text: No phase 3 placebo-adjusted biomarker data available (trial stopped before full results); calculator relies on phase 2 placebo-adjusted data from a different trial (ERN/LRPT) with unspecified background therapy.

against.text: Phase 2 placebo-adjusted data at 2g dose (matching AIM-HIGH max dose) available for all key biomarkers; baseline levels from AIM-HIGH itself; trial design parameters well documented.

hypotheses.would_settle: Publication of AIM-HIGH full results with placebo-adjusted biomarker changes.

issues.issue: Calculator input 'pathway' is null; niacin is a lipid-modifying agent acting via GPR109A to alter HDL-C, LDL-C, TG, Lp(a). Should be set to 'lipid' for correct calculator routing and assumption tracking.
issues.request: Set pathway to 'lipid' in calculator inputs.

issues.issue: Verifier SQL returned 'not_found' for LDL-C baseline (71 mg/dL, fact f_b280d226870380) and triglycerides baseline (161 mg/dL, fact f_4e489f41b1a507) from pmcid:PMC3120223, though both facts exist in the verified fact store. This discrepancy must be resolved before finalizing inputs.
issues.request: Re-run verifier queries for LDL-C and triglycerides baseline in AIM-HIGH (pmcid:PMC3120223) to confirm 71 mg/dL and 161 mg/dL; if confirmed, update verifier status.

issues.issue: ERN/LRPT phase 2 trial (pmid:19166443) background therapy is not specified in calculator inputs. AIM-HIGH enrolled patients on simvastatin with LDL-C 40-80 mg/dL; if ERN/LRPT patients were not on statins, the placebo-adjusted lipid changes may overestimate effects in a statin-treated population.
issues.request: Search for ERN/LRPT background lipid-lowering therapy (statin use, dose) and document in calculator input 'method' field.

issues.issue: AIM-HIGH niacin dose was titrated 1-2 g daily (mean ~1.5 g), while ERN/LRPT used fixed 2 g. The phase 2 placebo-adjusted changes at 2 g may overestimate the average on-treatment effect in AIM-HIGH.
issues.request: Note dose difference in calculator input 'method' field; consider sensitivity analysis using 1.5 g dose if phase 2 data available.
